Tumor cells with a high potential for proliferation are first identified and eliminated, while cancer stem cells (CSCs) continue to live. A small percentage of tumor cells undergo therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which can alter the tumor microenvironment and have tumorpromoting effects. CSCs can result in tumor relapses and are resistant to treatment [6]. CSCs are present in breast cancer, with studies showing that xeno-transplanted cell subpopulations enriched for CSCs can produce tumors from a small fraction of unselected cells [7]. The CSC hypothesis suggests that cancer recurrence and metastasis are caused by this particular subpopulation of cells, as they are the only ones capable of forming tumors. Isolating candidate CSCs is essential to showcasing their functional traits, which has been made possible by the application of cell-surface markers and labeling of cells that display stemness-related traits. The discovery of CSCs in 1994 was made possible through various studies, including the identification of a small subset of cells proliferating slower than the mature blast cells [4]. Cancer is a complex and heterogeneous disease, with treatment failures and individual differences in effectiveness affecting overall survival rates. This highlights the need for personalized, targeted anticancer treatments to overcome these challenges. precision medicine involves measuring key tumor characteristics to determine the best therapeutic plan for each patient, effectively treating their cancer and preventing relapse [13,14]. The use of novel molecular analysis in cancer research has led to extensive data gathering. This article examines recent developments in precision medicine for BC, a frequent and fatal disease, focusing on the function of stem cells and BCSCs in this regard. This review also covers the present understanding of BCSC biomarkers, their relative abundance, and clinical significance in BC, techniques for BCSC identification and isolation, the mechanism controlling BCSCs and their potential for therapeutics, regarding the origins of BCSCs, and approaches for investigating BCSC lineage in precision oncology. Origin of BCSCs The origin of tumors can be influenced by various factors, including the type of tumor, the type of stem cells, and the type of cell type [15]. Tissue-resident stem cells or their offspring may be the primary source of tumor start, which can occur during tissue regeneration, response to toxins, radiation, infections, or metabolic factors that result in mutations [5]. Tumor suppressors are inactivated, and oncogenes are overexpressed during the transformation process, allowing cells to proliferate out of control [16]. Tissue-resident stem cells have an infinite capacity for expansion, making them a potential source of tumors. Lineage tracing is a commonly employed method to monitor the movement, reproduction, and specialization of particular cells. Lineage tracing involves identifying all descendants of a single cell. Traditional single-cell lineage tracing assays have been the gold standard for determining the origin of a tumor. Still, this approach has limitations due to its reliance on a few markers [15]. The field of studying BCSC genesis has expanded with the advent of single-cell transcriptomics and single-cell genetic lineage tracing. The main theories about the development of BCSCs are the progenitor cells’ mutation-induced pluripotency into cancer stem cells (Fig. 1), the dedifferentiation of adult mammary cells into stem cells through the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and the generation of BCSCs from normal stem cells [4,17]. The hierarchical or CSC model assumes that only a tiny percentage of stem/progenitor cells within a tumor can replicate the tumor and reinforce the tumor hierarchy. In the linear hierarchy model of CSC creation, cancer is driven by transformation events in a stem or progenitor cell, leading to the development of more differentiated progeny as the tumor progresses. The offspring with distinct characteristics have a decreased ability to grow tumors. BCSCs have characteristics similar to minimally differentiated progenitor cells, including self-renewal, proliferation, and differentiation [4,18]. Research also indicates that differentiated mammary cells may become CSCs when exposed to harmful environmental factors like radiation and chemotherapy [19]. This hypothesis, known as clonal evolution or the stochastic model, postulates that all tumor cells have a comparable capacity to cause tumors and that intratumoral clonal evolution, caused by a series of mutations, results in tumor heterogeneity [20]. Cell stem cells in solid malignancies have a unidirectional hierarchy, meaning only the CSC population may prevent a tumor from growing. The clonal evolution model suggests that genetically unstable cells accumulate genomic and genetic alterations over time, leading to increased tumor aggressiveness, resistance, and heterogeneity [21]. The cellular plasticity model postulates that various cellular states can interconvert, explaining why these models are not mutually exclusive [22]. The lineage tracing test in mice models is currently the gold standard for defining the origin of BCSCs, enabling tracking of an animal singlecell clone by labeling different cell subpopulations with different cellspecific promotors [4]. The most popular method for monitoring the migration, division, and proliferation of certain cells in vivo is lineage tracing. From a molecular and cellular biology standpoint, lineage tracing has broadened the platforms accessible for drug screening, cell plasticity research, disease model building, and the development of customized medicine. Lineage tracing offers fresh perspectives on the growth and regeneration of digestive organs as well as methods for identifying the etiology and course of digestive diseases. However, recent developments in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have enabled the objective characterization of molecular states and cell identities in heterogeneous tissues at an unprecedented resolution [23]. Methods for the identification and isolation of breast cancer stem cells Four primary methods are used for identifying and isolating BCSCs are based on their functional characteristics or high expression of cell surface markers [4]. A popular technique is based on specific cell surface indicators or combinations of biomarkers, which is a top focus in cancer research (Table 1). Other techniques, such as mammosphere formation, ALDEFLUOR assay, and side population cell isolation using Hoechst 33342, are based on intrinsic properties of CSCs, such as high expression of ALDH1, ATP-binding cassette transporters, and CSC self-renewal and proliferation [4]. 4. Therapy-induced senescence: its hallmarks, biomarkers, and its role in BCSC generation Senescence is a process in cancer cells that occurs when exposed to DNA damage agents like radiation and chemotherapy [30,31]. This process, known as tumor suppressor senescence (TIS), has been extensively studied due to its significant impact on patients’ long-term outcomes. TIS is initiated and maintained by activating one or more tumor suppressor pathways, such as p53, p16 (Ink4a), p21 (Waf1), and retinoblastoma (RB) [5]. Cancer cells deficient in functional p53 and RB protein can still cause the senescence phenotype. Senescence and TIS have negative effects on treatment outcomes and prognoses, but they also attract immune cells, cause inflammation, and eliminate senescent tumor cells [5]. However, senescence can enhance CSC development by playing a significant pro-tumorigenic role. Classical biomarkers of cellular senescence include senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-ß-gal) activity, p53 protein expression, nuclear p53 concentration, p14 (Arf), p16 (Ink4a), and p21 (Waf1) upregulation, SASP, and frequently senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) [5]. Senescent cells also exhibit levels of heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) gamma, histone H3 di- or tri-methylated lysine 9 (H3K9Me2/3), and histone H2A variant (macroH2A) [32]. To accurately evaluate the pathological fate of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), it is necessary to verify the concurrent expression of several markers associated with the p53 pathway [33]. In cancers, innate and adaptive immune cells form a ‘senescence surveillance’ mechanism when induced, preventing premalignant cells from undergoing cancer growth [31,34]. More research is needed to demonstrate the significance of the chemokine axis in initiation and maintenance of senescence and ensure adequate immune surveillance. Signaling pathways such as Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and Hippo play a crucial role in regulating the self-renewal of BCSCs. The Notch signaling pathway is a crucial signaling cascade involved in the preservation of the BCSC phenotype [43]. It is essential for self-renewal, stem cell maintenance, and cellular differentiation during the developmental stage of cells. Notch signaling controls stem cell proliferation and differentiation into luminal progenitor cells in the mouse mammary gland. In the xenograft model, γ-secretase inhibition prevented the development of the active Notch intracellular domain (NCID), thereby stopping tumor growth [44] and decreasing the populations of CD44+/CD24� /low and ALDH + BCSCs. Overexpression of the Notch ligand DLL1 leads to increased Notch signaling, which in turn stimulates angiogenesis, migration, proliferation, and the CSC phenotype [45]. The abbrent Wnt/ β-catenin signaling system supports the renewal, proliferation, and differentiation of BCSC. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is one of the most important mechanisms controlling stem cell division and self-renewal [46,47]. Oncogenic stimulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases the development of human mammospheres and enriches mammary stem and progenitor cells. Wnt signaling contributes to BC chemoresistance and radioresistance, but blocking Wnt/β-catenin signaling inhibits the CSC-like phenotype, which reduces breast cancer metastasis [48]. The Canonical Wnt signaling pathway, which relies on β-Catenin and T cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancer factor (LEF), primarily regulates breast cancer cell proliferation and the maintenance of ’stemness’. Notch signaling regulates the differentiation of breast epithelial cells in the course of normal development. Different studies have shown that the Notch system significantly contributes to the advancement of breast cancer by involving the overexpression and/or aberrant genetic expression of notch receptors and ligands, which regulate angiogenesis. Hypoxia-induced up-regulation of Notch ligands led to the activation of Notch signaling. HIF-2α facilitated the transformation of stem cell characteristics by stimulating Notch and Wnt pathways in breast cancer cells. HIF-2α overexpression can trigger both Wnt and Notch signaling, which in turn supports the stem cell phenotype, treatment resistance, and overexpression of BCSC markers [49]. The hedgehog (Hh) pathway is a major regulator of cell fate and plays a significant role in cellular activities during embryonic development [50]. Proliferation, migration, metastasis, and aggressiveness of BC have all been linked to overexpression of the major Hh pathway regulators, SHH, DHH, PTCH1, and GLI1. The Hh/GLI signalling pathway involves ligands (Shh, Ihh, and Dhh), transmembrane receptors (Ptch1 and Ptch2), transcription factors (GLI1-3), and signalling regulators that collaborate to either inhibit or stimulate (Shh, Ihh, Dhh, SMO, GLI1-3) the signalling process. There was significant variation in the expression of Hippo genes among different subtypes of breast cancer. DNA methylation may regulate the Hippo pathway in breast cancer cells. The Hippo pathway, crucial for organogenesis and regeneration [51], is another significant circuit involving CSCs. It consists of a core transcriptional module and a core regulatory kinase module. The Hippo pathway is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis by balancing proliferation and differentiation. The pathway functions via a series of kinases that ultimately activate the Yes-associated protein (YAP) and its paralog, the transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ). TAZ is a transcriptional regulator that is often activated in human cancers. Recent studies show that TAZ is crucial for the development or progression of the majority of solid tumours. Their activation triggers the characteristics of cancer stem cells, including proliferation, resistance to chemotherapy, and the spread of cancer to other parts of the body. TAZ expression is significantly higher in tumors generated from BCSCs than in tumors not derived from BCSCs [52]. The BCSC pool’s upkeep has been linked to the interaction between TAZ and the extracellular matrix. Treatment with Dasatinib, a multi-target kinase inhibitor, demonstrated the ability to destroy the CSC population selectively [53]. Dasatinib belongs to a category of drugs known as kinase inhibitors. It functions by inhibiting the activity of an aberrant protein that stimulates cancer cells to proliferate. This inhibits the proliferation of cancer cells. Dasatinib enhances the sensitivity of KRAS-mutant cancer cells to mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase inhibitor via inhibiting TAZ activity. 6. New targeted approaches and therapeutic drugs targeting BCSC subpopulations Two hypotheses explain how BCSCs become multidrug resistance (MDR) in BC that show elevated resistance to standard chemotherapy treatments [5]. The first hypothesis suggests that only BCSCs expressing ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABC transporters) can repopulate the tumor by asymmetrical cell division following exposure to anticancer drugs. The second hypothesis suggests that only BCSCs survive chemotherapy and evolve new, more aggressive cell morphologies due to accumulated mutations [5]. Research on CSCs has been a topic of interest, with some strategies combining CSC-targeted treatments with traditional non-targeted therapies (Table 3). Kinase inhibitors and targeting Wnt and β-catenin pathways are two strategies for CSCtargeted treatments, some of which have reached clinical stage [47,62]. Immunological strategies targeting CSCs by MHC-restricted death include vaccination, antibody-based strategies, checkpoint inhibitor targeting, and adoptive cell transfer. MHC-unrestricted killing can occur through chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell methods, which are currently used when first-line medicines fail. CAR T-cellbased therapies have advanced into solid malignancies [63] due to their promising outcomes in hematological disorders. CAR T-cells are Tlymphocytes that have been genetically modified to target a specific antigen without being constrained by HLA, combining the specificity of antibodies with the activity of T-cells. The rising evidence that CSCs contribute to cancer development and recurrence suggests that developing anti-CSC medicines will likely enhance cancer patients’ long-term survival rates. A proof of principle for targeting CSCs was demonstrated in Acute myeloid leukemia (AML, a type of cancer that starts in the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow), where the anti-leukemia medication TDZD-8 selectively destroyed leukaemia stem cells while not impacting normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells [67]. Many of the mechanisms now being investigated as possible therapeutic targets in CSCs have been proven to govern normal stem and progenitor cells, thus identifying techniques to selectively target the pathways in cancer including breast cancer will be crucial. Recent research has focused on Notch and Wnt pathways as regulators of cell destiny in the breast [68-71]. It’s not surprising that they could be therapeutic targets in CSCs. In a model of Notch1-driven mammary carcinogenesis, inhibiting Notch signaling caused tumor regression and decreased tumorsphere development in vitro [72]. In response to hypoxia, the Notch ligand Jagged2 was upregulated in breast cancer cells and bone marrow derived cells, resulting in CSC growth [73]. Notch 4 activity is increased in breast CSCs, and Notch and Wnt signaling were found to mediate radio-resistance in breast progenitor and CSCs [74-76]. Pygo2, a Wnt co-activator, augmented mammosphere formation in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells [77]. In contrast, pygo2 deletion in MMTV-Wnt1 tumor cells reduced both mammosphere and tumor-forming capability [78]. The discovery of Salinomycin in a screen for CSC inhibitors highlighted the potential therapeutic value of targeting Wnt signaling. Salinomycin selectively eliminates CSCs by blocking Wnt signaling and triggering apoptosis [79-81]. Salinomycin also destroyed iCSCL-10A cells resistant to Taxol and Actinomycin D [82]. Metformin, an antidiabetic medicine, also appears to be effective against CSCs. Metformin targets CSC and can work together with chemotherapeutic medications to lower CSC levels and tumor progression [83,84]. Metformin inhibits NF-κB nuclear translocation and STAT3 phosphorylation in CSCs, relative to non-CSCs (Hirsch et al., 2013). Metformin may be effective for treating TAM-resistant ER + malignancies that upregulate NF-κB [85]. Metformin therapy successfully overcome Herceptin™ resistance in a Her2-positive xenograft model [86]. Predictive biomarkers can accurately assess the effectiveness of anticancer treatment strategies early in treatment, allowing for the appropriate modification of treatment regimens and selection of the most appropriate therapeutic intervention [98,99]. By studying patient groups with low treatmentoutcome prediction rates, more information on “interpersonal disease variations” can be used to customize anticancer treatment. The identification of stem cell markers in vivo and in vitro, along with the clarification of unique biological and metabolic traits of CSCs, has demonstrated their significant contribution to cancer progression, metastasis, chemoresistance, and tumor recurrence. A recent study explored the potential of ovarian CSC population targeting in relation to the effectiveness of anticancer agents like Cisplatin combined with ALDH targeting compounds or JAK2 inhibitors [100]. Research has shown the diversity in responses of multiple human BC cells to different anticancer agents, with the expression levels of molecular markers of BCSCs being correlated with the chemotherapeutic effect of anticancer agents. The potential use of CSCs and their markers in the customization of treatment regimens in breast neoplasia suggests the potential of using CSCs and their markers in pre- and post-chemotherapy initiation [101,102]. CSCs play a crucial role in factors such as tumorigenicity, metastasis, chemo/radioresistance, and multidrug resistance in anticancer treatment. Research has focused on molecules associated with CSCs that function as markers of recognition and differentiation and targets for their selective treatment. CSC markers may be crucial for their identification or targeting, and they can serve as valuable tools for treatment tailoring [101]. The variability in the chemotherapeutic/ cytotoxic effect of anticancer agents in human BC cells is correlated with the expression levels of several molecular markers of BCSCs, suggesting that these markers may be used as biomarkers in the fight against BC. 10. Conclusions and future perspectives The study examines the expression of potential CSC markers in primary breast carcinomas, finding that all markers had a high correlation with negative ER status. Additional markers are needed for IHC quantification of CSCs in ER + tumors, which account for 75-80 % of all breast cancers. The most potent predictor of outcome in ER-disease was a composite score representing the expression of all four markers, although only ITGA6 maintained independent prognostic relevance. Research BCSCs has made substantial progress in understanding their role in tumor development, spread, metastasis, medication resistance, and recurrence. Current therapies target BCSC signaling pathways and factors that preserve BCSC features, but their exact origins remain unknown. Recent advancements in single-cell genetic/epigenetic lineage tracing, single-cell transcriptomics technology, and computational algorithms for lineage reconstruction and differentiation trajectories could lead to the identification of the origin of BCSCs. Targeted therapies for BCSCs have been developed, with post-therapeutic local biopsies being particularly beneficial for identifying therapeutically targetable targets in residual tumor tissue and assessing the likelihood of tumor relapse based on multivariate biomarkers. Targeted therapies, such as immunotherapies, CAR NK, and CAR T cells, can be part of this secondary specific therapy. A potential

Targeted therapies, such as immunotherapies, CAR NK, and CAR T cells, can be part of this secondary specific therapy. A potential strategy to reduce the off-target effects of chemotherapy drugs and improve patient outcomes in the clinic is precision medicine. This is an essential method for treating breast cancer successfully. In order to anticipate the effectiveness of targeted therapy in particular patient groups, precision medicine necessitates the selection of appropriate biomarkers. Numerous potentially druggable mutations in breast tumours have been found, which could be used to build new therapies for breast cancer patients. Developments in omics technologies have concentrated on the more precise tactics of precision therapy. The advancement of next-generation sequencing technologies has stoked expectations for breast cancer treatment plans based on precision medicine. Additionally, focusing on BCSCs and signalling pathways may be a useful strategy for treating breast cancer. When combined with suitable single modalities, combination therapy techniques have the potential to greatly enhance the precision medicine treatment of metastatic BC. It has been difficult to create predictive BCSC biomarker markers, nevertheless, and more research is required. Patients’ chances of survival will increase with the advancement and application of nextgeneration sequencing technology as well as additional clinical studies including precision medicine-based treatments for breast cancer. The use of BCSCs in metastatic breast cancer therapy could be revolutionised by precision-medicine techniques. The field of precision medicine for life-saving breast cancer therapy must be advanced by coordinated efforts by researchers, medical professionals, and regulatory agencies. 11. Breast Cancer Treatment Local treatments Surgery for Breast Cancer Learn about surgery to treat breast cancer and access more information about lumpectomy and mastectomy, the two main types of surgery used. Radiation for Breast Cancer Different types of treatment are available for breast cancer. You and your cancer care team will work together to decide your treatment plan, which may include more than one type of treatment. Your treatment options may include both local and systemic treatments. Local treatments, such as surgery and radiation, are directed at the area with cancer and not the whole body. Systemic treatments, such as chemotherapy, are drugs that can reach cancer cells throughout the body. There are different treatment approaches for each type and stage of breast cancer. To learn more about treatment for specific types and stages of breast cancer, review What kind of treatment will I receive? below. Consulte Tratamiento del cáncer de mama (seno) para obtener información sobre el tratamiento del cáncer de mama en español. Join a Clinical Trial Joining a clinical trial may be an option. There are different types of clinical trials for people with breast cancer. You can use the clinical trial search to find NCI-supported cancer clinical trials that are accepting participants. You can also review a list of all current NCI-supported Breast Cancer Clinical Trials. For help finding a clinical trial, contact NCI’s Cancer Information Service. 1/3

You may receive radiation therapy as part of your breast cancer treatment. Learn about the types of radiation therapy and possible side effects. Systemic treatments Chemotherapy for Breast Cancer Not everyone with breast cancer will get chemotherapy. Learn about who gets chemo and why and find a list of drugs that may be prescribed. Hormone Therapy for Breast Cancer Hormone therapy helps lower the risk of recurrence of certain types of breast cancer. Learn about types of hormone therapy, common side effects, and more. Immunotherapy for Breast Cancer Immunotherapy may be used to treat triple-negative breast cancer. Learn about immunotherapy, when it is given, and common side effects. Targeted Therapy for Breast Cancer Targeted therapy is a treatment for certain types of breast cancer. Learn about types of targeted therapy, common side effects, and more. What kind of treatment will I receive? Breast Cancer Treatment by Stage The stage of breast cancer is an important factor in determining which type of treatment may work best for you. Learn more about treatment options for breast cancer by stage. Breast Cancer During Pregnancy Learn about breast cancer during pregnancy, including challenges in detection and options for treatment in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. 2/3

Inflammatory Breast Cancer Treatment Inflammatory breast cancer treatments may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and more. Learn about the different ways inflammatory breast cancer can be treated. Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Treatment Triple-negative breast cancer treatments may include surgery, chemotherapy, and more.
